NOW.what: Sells a workflow platform that automates IT, HR, customer service and now AI agent operations for large enterprises.
NOW.rev: Subscription revenue is over 97%. Public sector and financial services are large verticals. North America ~62%.
NOW.gm: Subscription gross margin around 81-83%. A single multi-instance platform serving very large contracts.
NOW.mgmt: Bill McDermott is CEO. Insider ownership small; renewal rates near 98% are the metric management points to.
NOW.comp: Salesforce, Atlassian, BMC and Microsoft in adjacent workflow; internal build for some processes.
NOW.moat: Once ServiceNow is the system of action for IT and HR workflows, replacing it means re-engineering how a company runs. Renewal rates near 98% show it.
NOW.ind: Enterprise workflow automation and AI agent budgets both growing.
NOW.risk: Seat-based pricing coming under pressure as AI reduces headcount in exactly the functions ServiceNow charges for.
NOW.implied: A very high multiple of earnings implies 20%+ subscription growth continuing for years with margins expanding.
NOW.debate: Bulls say it becomes the control plane for enterprise AI agents. Bears say the law of large numbers plus seat-based pricing risk catch up.
NOW.disprove: Current remaining performance obligation growth slowing below 18%; renewal rate falling; large deal count declining; AI product pricing not landing.

DHR.what: Sells bioprocessing equipment and consumables, diagnostics systems and life science instruments to biopharma and hospitals.
DHR.rev: Biotechnology (bioprocessing) ~25%, life sciences ~25%, diagnostics ~50%. Recurring consumables are the majority of revenue.
DHR.gm: Gross margin around 58-60%, higher than peers because of the consumables mix and the Danaher Business System cost discipline.
DHR.mgmt: Rainer Blair is CEO. The Rales family remains influential; the Danaher Business System is a genuine operational culture.
DHR.comp: Thermo Fisher, Sartorius, Merck KGaA in bioprocessing; Roche and Abbott in diagnostics.
DHR.moat: Validated bioprocessing consumables written into drug manufacturing filings - changing supplier means regulatory re-validation, so customers do not.
DHR.ind: Bioprocessing is recovering from destocking; diagnostics is steady; China remains weak.
DHR.risk: Biotech funding staying tight and pharma cutting R&D, so bioprocessing orders never return to trend.
DHR.implied: A high-20s P/E implies bioprocessing returns to high single-digit growth.
DHR.debate: Bulls say the consumables annuity plus the business system make it a quality compounder at a discount to history. Bears note organic growth has been roughly flat for three years.
DHR.disprove: Bioprocessing orders not recovering; China revenue declining further; respiratory diagnostics normalising lower; organic growth below 3% again.

TJX.what: Sells branded apparel and home goods at discount prices through TJ Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods - buying opportunistically from excess inventory.
TJX.rev: Marmaxx (US apparel) ~50%, HomeGoods ~17%, TJX Canada and International the rest. US around 75%.
TJX.gm: Gross margin around 30-31%. Off-price buying at discounts, low advertising spend and fast inventory turns make the model work.
TJX.mgmt: Ernie Herrman is CEO. Insider ownership small; the buying organisation is the real asset.
TJX.comp: Ross Stores, Burlington, Amazon and the full-price retailers whose excess inventory TJX buys.
TJX.moat: A buying network of over 21,000 vendors, scale that lets it absorb any lot size, and a treasure-hunt store experience that resists online replication.
TJX.ind: Off-price keeps taking share from department stores, and does well when consumers trade down.
TJX.risk: Tariffs and supply chain normalisation reducing the availability of cheap excess inventory, which is the raw material of the model.
TJX.implied: A high-20s P/E implies mid single-digit comparable sales growth continuing and margins holding.
TJX.debate: Bulls say it wins in both good and bad consumer environments. Bears say the multiple is full for a retailer and tariffs complicate sourcing.
TJX.disprove: Comparable sales below 3%; merchandise margin declining; inventory availability commentary turning negative; new store productivity falling.

ISRG.what: Sells the da Vinci surgical robot systems, and the instruments and services that every procedure consumes.
ISRG.rev: Instruments and accessories ~60% and recurring, systems ~25%, services ~15%. Roughly 70% US.
ISRG.gm: Gross margin around 66-68%. The razor-and-blade model: systems seed the installed base, instruments generate recurring high-margin revenue per procedure.
ISRG.mgmt: David Rosa is CEO, succeeding Gary Guthart. Insider ownership small; the company reinvests heavily in surgeon training and new platforms.
ISRG.comp: Medtronic Hugo, J&J Ottava, CMR Surgical - all trying to break a near-monopoly that has held for twenty years.
ISRG.moat: Surgeon training and habit, hospital capital already sunk, procedure data, and an instrument ecosystem. Surgeons trained on da Vinci do not switch easily.
ISRG.ind: Robotic surgery penetration is still low in most procedure categories - a long runway.
ISRG.risk: A credible competitor winning approvals and undercutting on price, or hospital capital budgets tightening.
ISRG.implied: A P/E near 60 implies procedure volume growth in the mid-teens continuing for many years with no share loss.
ISRG.debate: Bulls say it is a monopoly on a growing surgical standard with a recurring revenue annuity. Bears say competition is finally arriving and the multiple leaves no margin for error.
ISRG.disprove: Procedure growth slowing below 12%; da Vinci 5 placements disappointing; a competitor winning a major hospital system; instrument pricing pressure.

BKNG.what: Runs online travel marketplaces - Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, OpenTable, Kayak - taking commission on accommodation and travel bookings.
BKNG.rev: Accommodation is the large majority of gross bookings; Europe is the historical stronghold, with Asia growing through Agoda.
BKNG.gm: Take rate around 14-15% of gross bookings, with EBITDA margins above 35%. Marketing spend is the main variable cost and the key discipline.
BKNG.mgmt: Glenn Fogel is CEO. Insider ownership small; the company has retired a very large share count over the past decade.
BKNG.comp: Airbnb, Expedia, Google Travel and hotel direct booking channels.
BKNG.moat: Two-sided network effects between millions of properties and travellers, plus brand search dominance in Europe.
BKNG.ind: Global travel demand keeps growing; the risk is that AI assistants become the new booking interface.
BKNG.risk: Google or an AI assistant intermediating the traveller before they reach Booking.com, which would turn a marketplace into a supplier.
BKNG.implied: A mid-20s P/E implies high single-digit bookings growth plus continued aggressive buybacks.
BKNG.debate: Bulls say enormous free cash flow, shrinking share count and the best European lodging supply. Bears say the traffic acquisition channel is controlled by Google and AI changes it.
BKNG.disprove: Room nights growth slowing; marketing spend rising as a share of bookings; direct traffic mix falling; take rate compression.

VRTX.what: Sells the only approved medicines for the underlying cause of cystic fibrosis, plus a gene therapy for sickle cell and a new non-opioid painkiller.
VRTX.rev: Cystic fibrosis franchise (Trikafta/Alyftrek) is roughly 90% of revenue. Casgevy and Journavx are the diversification attempts. US ~60%.
VRTX.gm: Gross margin around 85-88% - among the highest in pharma. A monopoly in a rare disease with no alternative therapy.
VRTX.mgmt: Reshma Kewalramani is CEO. Insider ownership small; R&D is focused on serial monopolies in defined biology.
VRTX.comp: None in cystic fibrosis today; Sionna and others are in development. In pain, the entire opioid and NSAID market.
VRTX.moat: A genuine monopoly protected by patents, deep biology expertise and the fact that treating nearly the whole addressable patient population leaves little room for a rival to run trials.
VRTX.ind: Cystic fibrosis is a fixed patient population - growth comes from label expansion and geographic reimbursement. Pain is a vast new market.
VRTX.risk: Concentration: any threat to the cystic fibrosis franchise - a competitor or a patent challenge - hits nearly all the revenue.
VRTX.implied: A P/E in the 20s-30s implies Journavx becoming a large product and the pipeline diversifying revenue away from cystic fibrosis.
VRTX.debate: Bulls say a protected cash monopoly funding shots on goal in pain and kidney disease. Bears say one product is 90% of revenue and the new launches are unproven.
VRTX.disprove: Journavx prescription uptake and payer coverage disappointing; a competitor CFTR modulator advancing; pipeline failures in kidney disease; CF revenue growth flattening.

PLD.what: Owns and develops logistics warehouses near major cities and leases them to retailers, parcel carriers and manufacturers.
PLD.rev: Rental income from roughly 1.2 billion square feet globally, plus a strategic capital (fund management) business. US is the majority.
PLD.gm: REIT economics: watch funds from operations per share, same-store net operating income growth and the spread between in-place and market rents.
PLD.mgmt: Hamid Moghadam co-founded and led the company for decades; Dan Letter is now CEO. Insider ownership modest.
PLD.comp: Other industrial REITs, private capital (Blackstone), and developers in each local market.
PLD.moat: Infill land near population centres that cannot be replicated - supply is constrained by zoning, not by capital. Plus data on rents nobody else has.
PLD.ind: E-commerce still drives warehouse demand, but a development wave in 2022-2023 created temporary oversupply.
PLD.risk: Tariffs and a goods recession cutting leasing demand while new supply is still being delivered.
PLD.implied: The price implies the mark-to-market on expiring leases keeps converting into double-digit rent growth.
PLD.debate: Bulls say in-place rents are far below market, guaranteeing growth as leases roll. Bears see vacancy rising and demand weakening.
PLD.disprove: Occupancy falling below 95%; net effective rent change on renewals declining; development starts outpacing leasing; the lease mark-to-market gap narrowing.

BMY.what: Sells oncology, haematology, immunology and cardiovascular medicines, in the middle of a large patent cliff.
BMY.rev: Legacy portfolio (Revlimid, Eliquis, Opdivo) declining; growth portfolio (Reblozyl, Camzyos, Breyanzi, Cobenfy) rising. US ~65%.
BMY.gm: Gross margin around 70-75%, pressured by the mix shift and by acquisition amortisation.
BMY.mgmt: Christopher Boerner is CEO. Insider ownership small; the company has done large deals to buy growth.
BMY.comp: Merck and AstraZeneca in oncology, Pfizer in cardiovascular, J&J in immunology.
BMY.moat: Patents and oncology trial infrastructure, but the moat is visibly eroding as key products lose exclusivity.
BMY.ind: Oncology and neuroscience are growing; the company-specific issue is replacing expiring revenue.
BMY.risk: Cobenfy and the growth portfolio failing to offset Eliquis and Opdivo losses, leaving a decade of declining revenue.
BMY.implied: A high single-digit to low-teens P/E implies the market expects revenue decline. The bar is low.
BMY.debate: Bulls say a very cheap multiple with a large dividend and an underrated schizophrenia launch. Bears say declining revenue is rarely a good place to invest.
BMY.disprove: Cobenfy uptake below expectations; growth portfolio not offsetting legacy declines; further large debt-funded acquisitions; dividend coverage weakening.

NEM.what: Mines gold, plus copper, silver and zinc as by-products, from operations across the Americas, Australia and Africa.
NEM.rev: Gold is roughly 85-90% of revenue. Tier-one assets in Nevada (joint venture with Barrick), Australia, Peru and Ghana.
NEM.gm: All-in sustaining cost per ounce is the metric - roughly $1,400-1,600 against a much higher gold price, so margins are currently very wide.
NEM.mgmt: Natascha Viljoen is CEO, succeeding Tom Palmer. Insider ownership small; the Newcrest acquisition was the big strategic bet.
NEM.comp: Barrick, Agnico Eagle, AngloGold Ashanti and gold ETFs as the alternative way to own the metal.
NEM.moat: Reserve quality and scale in a business with no pricing power - the only durable advantage is low cost per ounce and long reserve life.
NEM.ind: Gold demand has been strong on central bank buying and currency debasement concerns.
NEM.risk: The gold price falling while costs stay elevated - miners lose money far faster than the metal falls.
NEM.implied: The multiple implies gold stays near current levels, which is a commodity bet, not a business bet.
NEM.debate: Bulls say it is operating leverage on a rising gold price plus free cash flow at last. Bears note decades of cost overruns and value destruction across the sector.
NEM.disprove: All-in sustaining costs rising above guidance; reserve replacement below production; a large acquisition at a high gold price; free cash flow not converting.

PGR.what: Sells personal auto and property insurance directly to consumers and through agents, pricing by telematics and data.
PGR.rev: Personal auto is the bulk, with property and commercial lines growing. US only.
PGR.gm: Combined ratio is the metric - Progressive targets 96 and has often delivered in the low 90s, meaning genuine underwriting profit before investment income.
PGR.mgmt: Tricia Griffith is CEO. Insider ownership small; the company is famously disciplined about pricing over growth.
PGR.comp: GEICO (Berkshire), State Farm, Allstate, plus Root and other insurtechs.
PGR.moat: Decades of driver data and segmentation models that price risk more accurately than rivals, plus brand and direct distribution scale.
PGR.ind: Auto insurance rates rose sharply after the claims inflation of 2022-23; the cycle is now softening.
PGR.risk: A soft pricing cycle: rivals cutting rates to win back share, forcing Progressive to choose between growth and margin.
PGR.implied: A mid-teens P/E implies the underwriting margin normalises rather than collapses as competition returns.
PGR.debate: Bulls say the best underwriter in US personal lines keeps taking share. Bears say margins are at cyclical peaks and rate cuts are coming.
PGR.disprove: Combined ratio rising above 96; policies in force growth slowing while rates fall; advertising spend rising without unit growth; severity trends re-accelerating.

COF.what: Issues credit cards to US consumers, lends on autos, and now owns the Discover network after the 2025 acquisition.
COF.rev: Domestic card is the majority of revenue, consumer banking (auto and deposits) and commercial banking the rest, plus Discover network fees.
COF.gm: Watch net interest margin (very high, card-driven), charge-off rates and the efficiency ratio.
COF.mgmt: Founder Richard Fairbank has run it since 1994 and holds a large stake - rare founder alignment in banking.
COF.comp: American Express, JPMorgan (Chase), Citi and Synchrony in cards.
COF.moat: Underwriting data on subprime and near-prime borrowers, and now ownership of a payment network - which is a genuinely different asset from being an issuer alone.
COF.ind: Card balances have grown strongly; credit normalisation after the pandemic is the key variable.
COF.risk: A consumer credit cycle hitting a card book that skews lower prime, while Discover integration is still underway.
COF.implied: The price implies Discover synergies land and charge-offs stay near current levels.
COF.debate: Bulls say owning a network transforms the economics and the stock is cheap on normalised earnings. Bears say subprime card losses rise fastest in a downturn.
COF.disprove: Net charge-offs rising above 6%; 30-day delinquencies climbing; Discover integration costs above plan; deposit costs rising.

FTNT.what: Sells network security appliances, SD-WAN and security software to mid-market and enterprise customers.
FTNT.rev: Product (appliances) plus service (subscriptions and support) - service is roughly 70% and recurring. Global, with strength in mid-market and EMEA.
FTNT.gm: Gross margin around 80-82%, unusually high for a hardware-inclusive vendor, because Fortinet designs its own security chips.
FTNT.mgmt: Co-founder Ken Xie is CEO and the Xie family holds a large stake - strong founder alignment.
FTNT.comp: Palo Alto Networks, Check Point, Cisco, Zscaler in secure access.
FTNT.moat: Custom ASICs give a price-performance advantage that competitors using general-purpose silicon cannot match, plus a large installed base and channel.
FTNT.ind: Firewall refresh cycles drive lumpy demand; SASE and OT security are the growth areas.
FTNT.risk: The firewall refresh cycle ending, as it did in 2023, leaving billings growth flat for a year.
FTNT.implied: A P/E in the 30s implies billings growth re-accelerating and unified SASE gaining share.
FTNT.debate: Bulls say the best margins in security with a hardware cost advantage. Bears say appliance-led security is structurally challenged by cloud-delivered rivals.
FTNT.disprove: Billings growth decelerating; product revenue declining; SASE and SecOps growth not offsetting firewall weakness; margin guidance cut.

GLW.what: Makes speciality glass and ceramics - optical fibre, display glass, Gorilla Glass and now optical connectivity for AI data centres.
GLW.rev: Optical communications (fastest growing, AI-driven), display technologies, speciality materials, environmental technologies and life sciences.
GLW.gm: Gross margin around 37-39%, improving as the optical mix grows. Manufacturing is capital-intensive with long asset lives.
GLW.mgmt: Wendell Weeks has been CEO since 2005. Insider ownership small; the company has a long record of patient R&D investment.
GLW.comp: Coherent and Lumentum in optical, AGC and Nippon Electric Glass in display, Chinese fibre manufacturers.
GLW.moat: Glass science know-how accumulated over 170 years, deep customer co-development (Apple in Gorilla Glass), and manufacturing processes that are hard to copy.
GLW.ind: AI data centre optical connectivity demand has transformed the growth outlook for the optical segment.
GLW.risk: The AI optical order surge proving to be an inventory build rather than sustained demand.
GLW.implied: A P/E in the 30s implies optical communications keeps growing at a high rate and display stays stable.
GLW.debate: Bulls say a slow-growth industrial has become an AI infrastructure supplier. Bears note the display business is mature and the optical cycle has turned before.
GLW.disprove: Optical communications order growth slowing; enterprise fibre demand normalising; display glass pricing falling; capex rising without revenue response.

SPGI.what: Rates debt issues, publishes market indices (S&P 500), and sells market data and commodity price benchmarks.
SPGI.rev: Ratings ~33% and the most profitable, market intelligence ~33%, indices ~13% with the best margins, commodity insights and mobility the rest.
SPGI.gm: Operating margins in the high 40s overall; the indices business runs above 65% because the index is a licence, not a product.
SPGI.mgmt: Martina Cheung became CEO in 2024. Insider ownership small; the company is planning to separate the mobility business.
SPGI.comp: Moodys in ratings, MSCI and FTSE Russell in indices, Bloomberg and FactSet in data.
SPGI.moat: A regulated duopoly in credit ratings, indices that are industry standards written into fund mandates, and data sets embedded in client workflows.
SPGI.ind: Debt issuance is cyclical; index and data revenue grow with assets and are highly recurring.
SPGI.risk: A prolonged freeze in debt issuance, which would hit the highest-margin ratings revenue directly.
SPGI.implied: A high-20s to 30s P/E implies mid-to-high single-digit revenue growth and continued margin expansion.
SPGI.debate: Bulls say it is a toll on global capital markets with near-monopoly positions. Bears note ratings revenue is cyclical and the multiple assumes issuance stays healthy.
SPGI.disprove: Billed issuance declining for multiple quarters; index assets under management growth slowing; market intelligence organic growth below 5%.

CVS.what: Runs retail pharmacies, a pharmacy benefit manager (Caremark) and a health insurer (Aetna) - the whole drug supply chain in one company.
CVS.rev: Health services (Caremark PBM) ~45%, health care benefits (Aetna) ~35%, pharmacy and consumer wellness ~20%. US only.
CVS.gm: Gross margin is low single digits to mid teens depending on segment - the PBM handles enormous revenue at thin spreads.
CVS.mgmt: David Joyner became CEO in late 2024 after Aetna underperformance. Insider ownership small; debt is significant.
CVS.comp: UnitedHealth/Optum, Cigna/Express Scripts, Walgreens, Amazon Pharmacy.
CVS.moat: Vertical integration and scale in drug purchasing - though it is a moat built on an intermediary role that politicians are actively attacking.
CVS.ind: Medicare Advantage margins have been under severe pressure; PBM economics face reform proposals.
CVS.risk: PBM reform legislation removing the spread and rebate economics that underpin the most profitable segment.
CVS.implied: A low-teens P/E implies partial Aetna margin recovery and PBM reform not being catastrophic.
CVS.debate: Bulls say a cheap multiple on a recovering insurer with an integrated pharmacy. Bears say the whole PBM business model is politically indefensible.
CVS.disprove: Aetna medical loss ratio not improving; PBM legislation advancing; Medicare star ratings falling; debt not being reduced.

LMT.what: Builds fighter aircraft (F-35), missiles, missile defence systems, helicopters and space systems for the US and allied governments.
LMT.rev: Aeronautics (F-35) ~40%, missiles and fire control ~17%, rotary and mission systems ~25%, space ~18%. US government is roughly 73% of sales.
LMT.gm: Operating margin around 10-11%. Cost-plus and fixed-price defence contracts cap profitability by design.
LMT.mgmt: Jim Taiclet is CEO. Insider ownership small; the F-35 programme dominates the strategic picture.
LMT.comp: RTX, Northrop Grumman, Boeing Defense, General Dynamics, plus new entrants like Anduril and SpaceX in space.
LMT.moat: Programme incumbency: once a platform is selected it runs for decades with sustainment revenue attached. Certification and security clearance barriers are absolute.
LMT.ind: Global defence spending is rising, especially in Europe, but US procurement priorities are shifting toward cheaper autonomous systems.
LMT.risk: F-35 procurement being cut in favour of unmanned systems, plus classified programme losses on fixed-price contracts.
LMT.implied: A high-teens P/E implies steady programme execution and international F-35 orders offsetting US budget shifts.
LMT.debate: Bulls say a rearming world buys more of exactly what Lockheed makes. Bears note charges on fixed-price programmes and a US preference for cheaper autonomy.
LMT.disprove: F-35 delivery or order reductions; further classified programme charges; free cash flow guidance cut; international orders not materialising.

MO.what: Sells cigarettes (Marlboro) and oral nicotine products in the United States only.
MO.rev: Smokeable products are roughly 88% of revenue; oral tobacco (on! and Copenhagen) the rest. It also holds a large stake in ABI.
MO.gm: Gross margin around 70%. Pricing power in an addictive category with no advertising costs allowed - the purest pricing machine in consumer goods.
MO.mgmt: Salvatore Mancuso is CEO, succeeding Billy Gifford. Insider ownership minimal; the dividend payout ratio is around 80% by policy.
MO.comp: Reynolds (BAT), ITG Brands, plus illicit disposable vapes which have taken real volume.
MO.moat: Marlboro brand loyalty and regulation that freezes market share by banning advertising - the moat is partly built by the regulator.
MO.ind: US cigarette volumes decline roughly 8-10% a year now, faster than historically, as illicit vapes take share.
MO.risk: Volume decline accelerating past the point where price increases can offset - the elasticity wall.
MO.implied: A low-teens P/E with a high dividend yield implies continued volume decline offset by pricing, with no growth.
MO.debate: Bulls collect a large, well-covered dividend from a business with no capital needs. Bears see terminal decline and failed attempts at nicotine alternatives (JUUL, NJOY).
MO.disprove: Shipment volumes declining more than 10%; net price realisation below 8%; on! growth stalling; FDA enforcement against illicit vapes failing.

PH.what: Sells motion and control technologies - hydraulics, filtration, aerospace systems - to industrial and aerospace customers.
PH.rev: Diversified industrial ~65%, aerospace systems ~35% and the highest-margin segment after the Meggitt acquisition. North America ~60%.
PH.gm: Gross margin around 35-37%. The aftermarket - replacement parts through distributors - is the profit engine, not original equipment.
PH.mgmt: Jenny Parmentier is CEO. Insider ownership small; the Win Strategy operating system has driven consistent margin expansion.
PH.comp: Eaton, Honeywell, Danaher in filtration, Safran and RTX in aerospace components.
PH.moat: Hundreds of thousands of engineered parts sold through a distribution network, with aerospace parts locked in by certification for the life of the aircraft.
PH.ind: Aerospace aftermarket is strong; general industrial demand has been soft.
PH.risk: An industrial recession while aerospace growth decelerates, exposing the leverage from the Meggitt debt.
PH.implied: A high-20s P/E implies aerospace margin expansion continues and industrial recovers.
PH.debate: Bulls say a proven margin-expansion machine with a growing aerospace annuity. Bears note industrial orders are weak and the multiple has re-rated a long way.
PH.disprove: Industrial orders declining; aerospace aftermarket growth slowing; margin expansion stalling; debt reduction slower than planned.

SBUX.what: Sells coffee and food through company-operated and licensed stores, mainly in the US and China.
SBUX.rev: North America ~75% of revenue, China ~8% and strategically important, international licensed the rest.
SBUX.gm: Store-level margins depend on labour and traffic; the North America operating margin has fallen sharply as labour investment increased.
SBUX.mgmt: Brian Niccol became CEO in 2024 to execute a turnaround after years of falling traffic. Insider ownership small.
SBUX.comp: Luckin Coffee in China, Dutch Bros and local independents in the US, McDonalds and convenience chains.
SBUX.moat: Brand, store density and the loyalty programme with tens of millions of active members - genuinely valuable but not preventing traffic decline.
SBUX.ind: US coffee traffic has been declining; China is intensely price-competitive.
SBUX.risk: The turnaround failing: traffic not returning while labour costs stay higher, so margins never recover.
SBUX.implied: A P/E in the 30s on depressed earnings implies a successful turnaround with margin recovery - the market is paying for the plan, not the results.
SBUX.debate: Bulls back Niccols record at Chipotle and see a brand that can be fixed. Bears note multiple quarters of negative comparable sales and a China business under structural attack.
SBUX.disprove: US comparable transactions still negative; China same-store sales declining; operating margin not recovering; loyalty member growth stalling.

APP.what: Sells an AI-driven advertising and monetisation platform to mobile app developers, and increasingly to e-commerce advertisers.
APP.rev: Advertising software platform is now almost all of revenue after the apps business was sold. Global, with a heavy games advertiser base.
APP.gm: Gross margin around 80%+ and EBITDA margins above 70% - extraordinary for an ad-tech business, driven by the Axon bidding engine.
APP.mgmt: Co-founder Adam Foroughi is CEO with a large stake. Aggressive buybacks have shrunk the share count meaningfully.
APP.comp: Meta and Google for advertiser budgets, Unity and ironSource in mobile game monetisation, The Trade Desk in broader programmatic.
APP.moat: The Axon machine learning model improves with data volume, and the install base of SDKs in mobile games creates a supply advantage.
APP.ind: Mobile advertising is growing; the e-commerce advertiser expansion is the new frontier and is unproven at scale.
APP.risk: Platform dependency - Apple or Google changing attribution or privacy rules could reset the model overnight - plus short-seller allegations about data practices.
APP.implied: A very high multiple implies the e-commerce expansion works and growth stays above 30% with 70%+ margins.
APP.debate: Bulls say a self-improving ad model with software margins and a founder who buys back stock. Bears point at platform dependency, short-seller reports and a very demanding multiple.
APP.disprove: Advertising revenue growth decelerating; e-commerce advertiser cohort churn; Apple or Google policy change; margins compressing.
